q.s: A 32-year-old woman has a routine ultrasound at 18 weeks' gestation. Her maternal serum α-fetoprotein was elevated. The fetal spine shows a posterior defect in the lumbosacral region with a fluid-filled sac containing neural tissue. She took no supplements before conception and has been taking valproate for epilepsy.
o: Herniation of the cerebellar tonsils only
Cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle
Failure of the posterior neuropore to close in week 4
Failure of the prosencephalon to divide
Failure of the anterior neuropore to close
e: Correct. Myelomeningocele; folate deficiency and valproate raise the risk.
q.ch: ↑ MSAFP + lumbosacral sac with neural tissue + valproate → failed posterior neuropore closure → myelomeningocele.
q.tr: Spina bifida occulta has normal AFP; open defects raise AFP and AChE.
q.q2: Which embryologic failure explains this defect?

q.s: A 2-year-old boy has headaches and vomiting. MRI shows the cerebellar tonsils and vermis herniated through the foramen magnum, aqueductal stenosis with hydrocephalus, and a lumbosacral myelomeningocele that was repaired at birth.
e: Wrong. Tonsils only, usually adults, often syringomyelia.
Wrong. Absent vermis with cystic fourth ventricle.
Correct. Vermis and tonsils herniate; associated with myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus.
q.ch: Tonsils + vermis through foramen magnum + myelomeningocele → Chiari II.
q.tr: Chiari I is tonsils only and presents in adulthood.
q.q2: Which malformation is this?

q.s: A 45-year-old man has had worsening burning pain in both hands for a year. On exam, he cannot feel pain or temperature over both shoulders and arms in a cape-like distribution, but fine touch and vibration are normal. He has wasting of the small muscles of his hands.
o: Anterior white commissure fibers of the spinothalamic tract
cl: fine touch and vibration are normal
wasting of the small muscles of his hands
q.ch: Bilateral cape-like pain and temperature loss + preserved dorsal columns + hand wasting → cervical syrinx → anterior white commissure, then anterior horns.
q.tr: Often associated with Chiari I.
q.q2: Which structure is damaged first?

q.s: A 70-year-old right-handed man suddenly cannot speak. He understands commands and follows them, but produces only a few effortful words. He is clearly frustrated. His right face and arm are weak; his leg is strong.
o: Superior division of the left middle cerebral artery
e: Correct. Broca area and lateral motor cortex.
cl: produces only a few effortful words
right face and arm are weak; his leg is strong
q.ch: Nonfluent aphasia + intact comprehension + right face/arm weakness → left MCA superior division.
q.tr: Lacunar strokes do not cause aphasia.
q.q2: Which artery is most likely occluded?

q.s: A 35-year-old man has tingling in his feet and weakness that began in his legs 5 days ago and has now spread to his arms. Three weeks ago he had diarrhea. On exam he has symmetric weakness, absent reflexes and mild bilateral facial weakness. His results are shown.
o: Molecular mimicry causing autoimmune demyelination of peripheral nerves
Destruction of anterior horn cells by virus
cl: began in his legs 5 days ago and has now spread to his arms
Three weeks ago he had diarrhea
q.ch: Ascending weakness after diarrhea + areflexia + high CSF protein with normal cells → Guillain-Barré (albuminocytologic dissociation).
q.tr: Watch for respiratory failure; treat with IVIG or plasmapheresis, not steroids.
q.q2: Which mechanism best explains his illness?

q.s: A 24-year-old woman has double vision. When she looks to the left, her right eye does not move past the midline and her left eye has horizontal nystagmus. When she focuses on a near object, both eyes converge normally. Two years ago she had an episode of painful vision loss that resolved.
e: Correct. Right INO from multiple sclerosis.
Wrong. Left eye would fail to adduct.
Wrong. Left eye would not abduct.
cl: her right eye does not move past the midline
her left eye has horizontal nystagmus
q.ch: Right adduction failure + left abducting nystagmus + normal convergence + prior optic neuritis → right MLF lesion → MS.
q.tr: INO is named for the eye that cannot adduct.
q.q2: Which structure is damaged?

q.s: A 65-year-old man with hypertension has sudden vertigo, nausea and difficulty swallowing. His voice is hoarse. His left pupil is small and his left eyelid droops. He has lost pain sensation on the left side of his face and the right side of his body. He cannot do left finger-to-nose testing accurately.
e: Wrong. Facial paralysis and deafness, no dysphagia.
cl: His left pupil is small and his left eyelid droops
left side of his face and the right side of his body
q.ch: Dysphagia + hoarseness + ipsilateral Horner + crossed pain loss + ipsilateral ataxia → lateral medulla → PICA.
q.tr: "Don't pick a horse (hoarseness) that can't eat (dysphagia)."
q.q2: Which artery is occluded?

q.s: A 54-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with confusion. His sodium is corrected with hypertonic saline as shown. On day 3 he develops difficulty speaking and swallowing and cannot move his arms or legs, though he can still blink.
e: Correct. Osmotic demyelination; sodium rose 24 mEq/L in 24 hours.
cl: cannot move his arms or legs, though he can still blink
q.ch: Hyponatremia corrected by 24 mEq/L in 24 h → osmotic demyelination of the pons → dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriplegia.
q.tr: "From low to high, your pons will die."
q.q2: Which lesion is most likely?

q.s: A 29-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 has daily headaches that are worse lying down and brief episodes where her vision goes gray. She takes isotretinoin for acne. Fundoscopy shows bilateral swelling of the optic discs. MRI is normal except for an empty sella. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cm H₂O with normal CSF.
e: Correct. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; also weight loss and stopping isotretinoin.
cl: bilateral swelling of the optic discs
opening pressure of 34 cm H₂O with normal CSF
q.ch: Obese woman + vitamin A derivative + papilledema + high opening pressure with normal imaging → IIH → acetazolamide.
q.tr: Untreated IIH can cause permanent vision loss.
q.q2: Which drug is first-line treatment?

q.s: A 76-year-old man has had trouble walking for 6 months. His feet seem glued to the floor. He has wet himself several times and his wife says he has become forgetful. CT shows enlarged ventricles without widened sulci.
o: Large-volume lumbar puncture to assess improvement
cl: His feet seem glued to the floor
He has wet himself several times
q.ch: Magnetic gait + incontinence + cognitive decline + ventriculomegaly → NPH → CSF drainage trial, then shunt.
q.tr: "Wet, wobbly and wacky," and one of the reversible dementias.
q.q2: What is the best next step?
q.fc: Family pedigree; numbers in parentheses are ages at symptom onset

q.s: A 29-year-old man has jerky, dance-like movements of his arms, irritability and difficulty planning tasks. His family is shown. MRI shows atrophy of the caudate nuclei with enlarged lateral ventricles.
o: Expansion of CAG trinucleotide repeats in HTT, especially through the father
q.ch: Chorea + psychiatric change + caudate atrophy + earlier onset each generation → Huntington → CAG expansion (anticipation).
q.tr: Neurotransmitters: ↑ dopamine, ↓ GABA, ↓ ACh.
q.q2: Why does the disease appear earlier in each generation?

q.s: A 69-year-old woman has a slow, shuffling gait, resting tremor of her right hand and rigidity. She is started on a drug. Months later she has visual hallucinations and develops lightheadedness on standing. Her symptoms improve for 2–3 hours after each dose, then return abruptly.
e: Correct. Hallucinations, postural hypotension and on-off phenomenon.
cl: improve for 2–3 hours after each dose, then return abruptly
q.ch: Parkinson + hallucinations + orthostasis + wearing-off fluctuations → levodopa/carbidopa.
q.tr: COMT and MAO-B inhibitors extend the "on" time.
q.q2: Which drug is she taking?

q.s: A 73-year-old man has 2 years of progressive forgetfulness. He repeats questions, gets lost in his neighborhood and cannot manage his finances. Neurologic exam is otherwise normal. MRI shows diffuse cortical atrophy, worst in the hippocampi.
o: Extracellular β-amyloid plaques and intracellular tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau
Round tau inclusions in frontal neurons
q.ch: Slow progressive memory loss + visuospatial deficits + hippocampal atrophy → Alzheimer → plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.
q.tr: The number of tangles correlates with severity.
q.q2: Which finding would be expected in his brain tissue?

q.s: A 66-year-old man has 6 months of dementia with fluctuating alertness. He reports seeing small animals in his room and has started acting out his dreams. Exam shows mild rigidity and slow movements. After being given haloperidol for agitation, he becomes very rigid.
e: Correct. Dementia with Lewy bodies; sensitive to antipsychotics.
cl: seeing small animals in his room
q.ch: Dementia + fluctuations + hallucinations + RBD + parkinsonism → Lewy body dementia → α-synuclein.
q.tr: Dementia within 1 year of parkinsonism points to Lewy bodies, not Parkinson disease dementia.
q.q2: Which protein forms inclusions in his cortical neurons?

q.s: A 64-year-old woman has had rapidly worsening confusion over 8 weeks. She now cannot walk and has sudden jerks when startled by noise. EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes. CSF shows elevated 14-3-3 protein.
o: Misfolded prion protein converting normal protein into a protease-resistant β-pleated form
cl: sudden jerks when startled by noise
q.ch: Rapid dementia + startle myoclonus + periodic sharp waves + 14-3-3 → CJD → PrPsc.
q.tr: Spongiform cortex without inflammation.
q.q2: What is the pathologic mechanism?

q.s: A 6-year-old girl's teacher reports that she "zones out" many times a day for a few seconds at a time, with eyelid fluttering. She does not fall and is immediately alert afterward. Breathing quickly for 3 minutes in clinic triggers an episode.
e: Wrong. Focal seizures; may worsen absence.
Correct. Blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels.
cl: "zones out" many times a day for a few seconds
q.ch: Frequent brief staring + no postictal phase + hyperventilation trigger → absence seizures (3-Hz spike-wave) → ethosuximide.
q.tr: "Sucks to have silent (absence) seizures."
q.q2: What is the best treatment?
q.fc: Steady-state drug level at increasing daily doses

q.s: A 42-year-old woman with focal seizures has been taking an anticonvulsant for years. She now has swollen gums that bleed easily and increased facial hair. Her drug levels at different doses are shown; her level rose sharply after a small increase in dose.
e: Correct. Zero-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.
cl: rose sharply after a small increase in dose
q.ch: Gingival hyperplasia + hirsutism + nonlinear kinetics → phenytoin.
q.tr: Folate supplementation helps prevent gingival hyperplasia.
q.q2: Which drug is she taking?

q.s: A 28-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy wants to become pregnant. She takes the drug that controls her seizures best.
e: Correct. Neural tube defects and highest teratogenicity.
q.ch: Generalized epilepsy + pregnancy planning → valproate has highest teratogenic risk → switch (e.g., lamotrigine or levetiracetam) and give folate.
q.tr: Valproate also causes hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis.
q.q2: Which drug carries the highest teratogenic risk and should ideally be changed?

q.s: A 37-year-old man has brief, intense pain behind his left eye each night for 2 weeks. Each attack lasts about an hour, with tearing, a runny left nostril and a droopy left eyelid. He paces the room during attacks. He had similar clusters last year.
cl: tearing, a runny left nostril and a droopy left eyelid
q.ch: Repetitive brief unilateral periorbital pain + autonomic symptoms + clusters → cluster headache → oxygen.
q.tr: Migraine patients lie still in a dark room; cluster patients pace.
q.q2: Which treatment aborts the acute attack?

q.s: A 19-year-old man hit in the temple with a baseball lost consciousness for a moment. In the emergency department he talks normally, but an hour later he becomes drowsy and his right pupil dilates. He develops weakness of his left arm and leg.
o: Biconvex (lens-shaped) collection limited by suture lines
e: Correct. Epidural hematoma from middle meningeal artery.
cl: talks normally, but an hour later he becomes drowsy
q.ch: Temple trauma + lucid interval + ipsilateral blown pupil + contralateral weakness → epidural hematoma → biconvex lens on CT.
q.tr: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery.
q.q2: Which finding is expected on CT?
q.fc: Lumbar puncture results; noncontrast CT 4 days after onset was read as normal

q.s: A 48-year-old woman with polycystic kidneys had the sudden "worst headache of her life" 4 days ago while lifting a box. She now has neck stiffness. Her results are shown.
e: Wrong. Prevented by securing the aneurysm.
q.ch: ADPKD + thunderclap headache + xanthochromia → SAH → nimodipine to prevent vasospasm.
q.tr: CT sensitivity falls after the first day; LP then decides.
q.q2: Which complication should be prevented with nimodipine?
q.fc: Bedside tuning fork and audiology results

q.s: A 34-year-old woman has gradual hearing loss in her left ear and imbalance. A tuning fork placed on her forehead is heard louder in her right ear. With the fork beside her left ear, she hears it better through the air than on the bone behind the ear. MRI shows an enhancing mass at the left cerebellopontine angle.
cl: heard louder in her right ear
Weber lateralizes away: left sensorineural loss.
hears it better through the air than on the bone
mass at the left cerebellopontine angle
q.ch: Left sensorineural hearing loss + CPA mass → vestibular schwannoma → Schwann cells.
q.tr: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas mean NF2 (chromosome 22).
q.q2: Which cell type gave rise to this tumor?

q.s: A 61-year-old man has had headaches for 2 months and his family says he is "not himself." MRI shows a large mass in both frontal lobes connected across the corpus callosum, with a necrotic center and ring enhancement. Biopsy shows atypical cells lined up around areas of necrosis.
o: It is a grade 4 astrocytoma with a median survival of about 15 months
It is benign with excellent prognosis
It is the most common childhood tumor
cl: atypical cells lined up around areas of necrosis
q.ch: Butterfly mass + central necrosis + pseudopalisading → glioblastoma.
q.tr: EGFR amplification is common.
q.q2: Which statement about this tumor is correct?

q.s: A 5-year-old boy has morning headaches with vomiting and a wide-based, unsteady gait. MRI shows a solid mass in the cerebellar vermis filling the fourth ventricle. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells forming rosettes around fibrillary material.
o: Seeding of the spinal subarachnoid space ("drop metastases")
cl: small round blue cells forming rosettes
q.ch: Vermis mass in a child + small blue cells + Homer-Wright rosettes → medulloblastoma → drop metastases.
q.tr: A cystic cerebellar mass with a mural nodule is pilocytic astrocytoma instead.
q.q2: Which complication is most characteristic of this tumor?

q.s: A 9-year-old girl has a 9-month history of headaches and bumps into things on both sides. She has grown little in the past year. CT shows a calcified cystic mass above the sella.
cl: bumps into things on both sides
She has grown little in the past year
calcified cystic mass above the sella
q.ch: Child + bitemporal field loss + growth failure + calcified suprasellar cyst → craniopharyngioma → Rathke pouch.
q.tr: Pituitary adenomas are uncommonly calcified.
q.q2: From which tissue does this tumor arise?

q.s: A 14-year-old boy has had progressive unsteadiness since age 10. He has absent reflexes in his legs, loss of vibration sense, extensor plantar responses, high-arched feet and a curved spine. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
cl: Dorsal root ganglia and peripheral nerves.
high-arched feet and a curved spine
q.ch: Childhood ataxia + areflexia with Babinski + pes cavus + scoliosis + HCM → Friedreich ataxia → GAA repeat in frataxin.
q.tr: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of death.
q.q2: Which gene is affected and how is it inherited?

q.s: A 50-year-old man has had weakness for a year. He has thin, twitching muscles in his hands, brisk reflexes and spasticity in his legs, and slurred speech. Sensation, eye movements and bladder function are normal.
cl: thin, twitching muscles in his hands
brisk reflexes and spasticity in his legs
Sensation, eye movements and bladder function are normal
q.ch: Mixed UMN + LMN signs with normal sensation → ALS → riluzole.
q.tr: Familial ALS may involve SOD1.
q.q2: Which drug may prolong his survival, and how does it work?

q.s: A 12-year-old girl has seizures and learning problems. She has light-colored leaf-shaped patches on her back, red bumps across her nose and cheeks, and a rough leathery patch of skin on her lower back. Renal ultrasound shows fat-containing masses.
o: Autosomal dominant; hamartin/tuberin inhibition of mTOR
cl: red bumps across her nose and cheeks
q.ch: Seizures + ash-leaf spots + angiofibromas + shagreen patch + AMLs → tuberous sclerosis → TSC1/TSC2 → mTOR.
q.tr: Also cardiac rhabdomyoma and SEGA.
q.q2: Which inheritance and pathway are affected?

q.s: A 58-year-old smoker has right shoulder and arm pain. His right eyelid droops slightly and his right pupil is smaller than the left, especially in dim light. His right forehead does not sweat. Chest imaging shows a mass at the right lung apex.
o: Third-order neuron along the internal carotid
Second-order neuron near the stellate ganglion
cl: smaller than the left, especially in dim light
His right forehead does not sweat
mass at the right lung apex
q.ch: Apical lung mass + ptosis + miosis + anhidrosis → second-order (preganglionic) Horner.
q.tr: Carotid dissection Horner is painful and usually spares facial sweating.
q.q2: Which neuron in the sympathetic pathway is damaged?

q.s: A 59-year-old woman with diabetes wakes with double vision. Her left eyelid droops and her left eye points down and out. The left pupil is equal in size to the right and reacts normally to light. She has no headache.
o: An aneurysm is compressing the nerve
The lesion is in the cavernous sinus
Ischemia affects central motor fibers while the peripheral parasympathetic fibers are spared
The lesion is in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Parasympathetic fibers run in the center of the nerve
q.ch: Diabetes + down-and-out eye + ptosis + normal pupil → ischemic CN III palsy → central motor fibers affected.
q.tr: A painful CN III palsy with a blown pupil is a PCom aneurysm until proven otherwise.
q.q2: Why is the pupil spared?

q.s: A 64-year-old woman leaves a dark restaurant and has sudden severe pain in her right eye with blurred vision, halos around lights, headache and vomiting. The right eye is red, the cornea is hazy and the pupil is mid-dilated and does not react to light.
e: Correct. Mydriatics worsen acute angle closure.
cl: mid-dilated and does not react to light
q.ch: Sudden painful red eye + halos + mid-dilated fixed pupil after dim light → acute angle-closure glaucoma → avoid mydriatics.
q.tr: "Hurts in a hurry with halos, a headache and a half-dilated pupil."
q.q2: Which drug should be avoided?

q.s: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped his anticoagulant has sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale, swollen retina with a bright red spot in the center of the macula.
o: The thin fovea lacks inner retinal layers, so the intact choroidal circulation shows through the surrounding pale, ischemic retina
cl: atrial fibrillation who stopped his anticoagulant
bright red spot in the center of the macula
q.ch: Embolic source + sudden painless monocular loss + pale retina with cherry-red spot → central retinal artery occlusion.
q.tr: Central retinal vein occlusion gives "blood and thunder" instead.
q.q2: Why does the fovea appear red?

q.s: A 50-year-old woman has spinning vertigo for a few seconds whenever she lies down or turns over in bed. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus. When her head is turned to the right and she is laid back quickly, she develops vertigo and a torsional, upbeating nystagmus that fades within 30 seconds.
cl: for a few seconds whenever she lies down or turns over
She has no hearing loss or tinnitus
q.ch: Brief positional vertigo + positive Dix-Hallpike + no hearing loss → BPPV → Epley maneuver.
q.tr: Ménière: vertigo for hours with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness.
q.q2: What is the best treatment?

q.s: A 3-year-old boy has had a fever and ear pain for 2 days after a cold. Today, the area behind his left ear is red, swollen and tender, and his left ear is pushed forward.
e: Correct. Spread of acute otitis media to mastoid air cells.
cl: fever and ear pain for 2 days after a cold
area behind his left ear is red, swollen and tender
his left ear is pushed forward
q.ch: Acute otitis media + postauricular swelling pushing the pinna forward → mastoiditis.
q.tr: Risks include subperiosteal abscess and meningitis.
q.q2: Which complication has occurred?
q.fc: Response to skin incision at increasing inhaled anesthetic concentrations

q.s: Two inhaled anesthetics are compared as shown. Agent Y is a gas that enters and leaves the blood very quickly and can expand air-filled spaces in the body.
o: Agent X has the faster induction
Agent Y has high lipid solubility
Agent X has a lower MAC, higher lipid solubility and greater potency
MAC is the concentration that causes apnea
Agent Y is more potent because its curve is to the right
e: Wrong. Agent Y has low blood solubility.
Correct. Potency = 1/MAC; agent Y behaves like nitrous oxide.
Wrong. Higher MAC means lower potency.
cl: enters and leaves the blood very quickly
q.ch: Left-shifted curve (MAC ≈ 1%) → lower MAC → more lipid soluble → more potent; agent Y ≈ N2O (MAC > 100%).
q.tr: Potency relates to lipid solubility; speed relates to blood solubility.
q.q2: Which statement is correct?

q.s: During laparoscopic surgery with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a 22-year-old man develops a stiff jaw and rigid limbs. His end-tidal CO2 rises steeply, his heart rate climbs to 140/min and his temperature reaches 40.5°C. His uncle died during surgery.
o: Blocks ryanodine receptors, preventing Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
q.ch: Volatile + succinylcholine + rigidity + hypercapnia + hyperthermia + family history → malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene.
q.tr: Antipyretics do not work because the set point is normal.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of the drug that should be given?

q.s: A 31-year-old woman on methadone maintenance is in labor and requests pain relief. Thirty minutes after an injection she becomes restless, with yawning, a runny nose, abdominal cramps and dilated pupils.
e: Wrong. Full agonist; would not cause withdrawal.
Correct. μ partial agonist/κ agonist displaces methadone.
cl: yawning, a runny nose, abdominal cramps and dilated pupils
q.ch: Methadone patient + mixed agonist/antagonist for labor pain → precipitated withdrawal → butorphanol or nalbuphine.
q.tr: Mixed agonist/antagonists cause less respiratory depression and are hard to reverse with naloxone.
q.q2: Which drug was most likely given?

q.s: A 45-year-old man with a lumbar laceration has a local anesthetic injected around the wound. A few minutes later he becomes cyanotic. Pulse oximetry reads 85% despite oxygen, and his arterial blood is chocolate brown with a normal PaO2.
cl: chocolate brown with a normal PaO2
q.ch: Local anesthetic + cyanosis unresponsive to O2 + chocolate blood + normal PaO2 → methemoglobinemia → prilocaine or benzocaine → methylene blue.
q.tr: Bupivacaine is the cardiotoxic one.
q.q2: Which drug was given, and what treats this?

q.s: A 30-year-old man is brought in unresponsive. He is breathing 5 times a minute with pinpoint pupils. Track marks are on his arms. He is given a drug and wakes up within a minute. Forty-five minutes later he is again difficult to arouse.
o: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids
e: Correct. Repeat doses or infusion may be needed.
cl: breathing 5 times a minute with pinpoint pupils
Forty-five minutes later he is again difficult to arouse
q.ch: Opioid overdose → naloxone reverses quickly but wears off before long-acting opioid → recurrent sedation.
q.tr: Tolerance never develops to miosis and constipation.
q.q2: Why did he become drowsy again?

q.s: A 72-year-old woman has 3 years of memory loss and is started on a drug. Two weeks later she develops nausea and episodes of lightheadedness. Her pulse is 46/min.
e: Correct. AChE inhibitor; vagal effects slow the heart.
q.ch: Alzheimer treatment + nausea + bradycardia → AChE inhibitor (donepezil).
q.tr: Avoid AChE inhibitors in patients with conduction abnormalities.
q.q2: Which drug was started?
